title: Federal Tax Research: A Guide to the IRC, Regulations, and Case Law
summary: A complete guide for tax professionals on the primary sources of U.S. federal tax law. Learn to navigate the IRC, Treasury Regulations, and judicial authority.
body_text: Behind every solid tax position is a paper trail of authority. Federal tax research is how you build it: finding the right sources of U.S. tax law, weighing them against each other, and applying them to the question in front of you. It's what turns "I think" into "I can show you why," and what keeps you compliant, protected, and able to defend your advice. That authority follows a hierarchy every practitioner should have reflexes for: Statute: the Internal Revenue Code Administrative guidance: Treasury regulations and IRS rulings Judicial interpretation: federal court decisions Each layer matters differently, and together they underpin everything from a routine return to an audit defense to a high-stakes planning memo. They also define the standard that shields you from penalties. Under Treas. Reg. §1.6662-4(d), you have substantial authority when the weight of support for your position is substantial against the weight pointing the other way. It's an objective bar set above "reasonable basis" but below "more likely than not." While federal law is uniform, practitioners must also navigate the complexities of state and local tax research . Combining federal and state-level analysis is often essential for multi-jurisdictional taxpayers . Want a broader framework for tackling every level of tax law? See our Ultimate Guide to Tax Research , which covers federal, state, international, and secondary sources. What Is the IRC? The Cornerstone of Statutory Authority in U.S. Tax Law The IRC, codified as Title 26 of the U.S. Code, is the bedrock of federal taxation in the United States. Enacted by Congress, it provides the comprehensive legal framework governing income, estate, gift, employment, and excise taxes, as well as taxpayer rights, enforcement procedures, and compliance requirements. As the highest statutory authority in the federal tax system, the IRC guides the interpretive roles of administrative agencies and courts, which add significant nuance to its application. Administrative guidance, such as regulations and rulings issued by the U.S. Treasury Department or IRS, must align with the IRC and can be invalidated by courts if found inconsistent. Notably, the deference courts give to that guidance changed significantly in 2024. In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo , 603 U.S. 369 (2024), the Supreme Court overruled Chevron and held that the Administrative Procedure Act requires courts to exercise independent judgment when deciding whether an agency acted within its statutory authority; courts may not defer to an agency interpretation merely because a statute is ambiguous. Agency interpretations may still be persuasive under Skidmore , especially when they are thorough, well-reasoned, consistent, and informed by agency expertise, and courts must still respect valid delegations of discretion from Congress. While courts do not create tax law in a legislative sense, they play a critical role in interpreting the IRC, resolving ambiguities, establishing binding precedents, and shaping its practical meaning. Given its foundational role, the IRC is the primary source that practitioners consult when evaluating a tax issue. Every credible analysis begins with the IRC, ensuring that interpretations and conclusions are grounded in its authoritative text. How the IRC Is Structured and Navigated The IRC is intentionally layered, with a hierarchy that mirrors how tax law is applied: Subtitles (e.g., Subtitle A – Income Taxes) Chapters (e.g., Chapter 1 – Normal Taxes and Surtaxes) Subchapters (e.g., Subchapter B – Computation of Taxable Income) Parts and Subparts (e.g., Part IX – Items Not Deductible) Sections (e.g., §179 – Deduction for Certain Depreciable Property) Each section of the IRC is legally binding. Many sections contain exceptions, special rules, or cross-references, creating a dense but logical system for organizing federal tax law. For instance, Section 121 allows for the exclusion of gain on the sale of a principal residence and is often interpreted in tandem with Treasury regulations. How Does Administrative Guidance Interpret the IRC? Translating Statutes Into Actionable Guidance Administrative authority consists of official interpretations and procedures issued by the U.S. Treasury Department and the IRS. These documents explain how to apply the IRC in real-world situations and guide both taxpayers and tax professionals through compliance, elections, and risk management. Treasury Regulations are the most authoritative form of administrative guidance and, when valid, are binding on both taxpayers and the IRS. Other forms of administrative guidance, often called sub-regulatory guidance, do not carry that level of authority. Since Loper Bright , courts no longer defer to Treasury or IRS interpretations merely because a statute is ambiguous. Instead, a reviewing court independently interprets the statute, recognizes any valid delegation of discretion to the agency, determines the boundaries of that delegation, and reviews whether the agency acted within those boundaries through reasoned decisionmaking. Agency guidance may still carry persuasive weight to the extent it is thorough, consistent, and well-reasoned (the Skidmore standard), but it no longer commands automatic deference. Even so, regulations and sub-regulatory guidance remain crucial for understanding how the law is interpreted and enforced, and many forms of sub-regulatory guidance are routinely cited to inform and support return positions, audit defenses, and planning strategies. Treasury Regulations Treasury regulations are the most authoritative form of administrative guidance. Issued by the Treasury Department under authority delegated by Congress, they explain how specific IRC provisions are to be implemented. Regulations come in three categories: Proposed regulations – Released for public comment; not binding. Taxpayers generally may not rely on proposed regulations unless the preamble expressly permits reliance Temporary regulations – Effective immediately; often used for time-sensitive issues; under IRC §7805(e), they expire within three years after the date of issuance (for temporary regulations issued after November 20, 1988) Final regulations – Carry full legal weight and are typically cited in legal and tax opinions For example, Treas. Reg. §1.121-3 interprets IRC section 121 and clarifies the safe harbor for partial exclusion of gain due to unforeseen circumstances. Final regulations like this are a core part of the federal tax research process. Revenue Rulings Revenue rulings are official IRS responses to specific factual scenarios. They show how the IRS would apply the law in similar cases and are published to guide taxpayers broadly, not just the person who submitted the original inquiry. While Revenue Rulings do not have the force and effect of Treasury Regulations, they are official IRS interpretations published in the Internal Revenue Bulletin and may be used as precedents, subject to later legislation, regulations, cases, rulings, and procedures. They are especially useful when analyzing recurring or unsettled issues. Revenue Procedures Revenue procedures set forth the administrative steps taxpayers must follow to comply with the law. These often include: Safe harbor guidelines Election procedures Relief methods for late filings or changes in accounting methods Unlike revenue rulings, which interpret the law, revenue procedures focus on how to comply. For example, a revenue procedure may describe how to request an automatic change in accounting method under Section 446. Chief Counsel Advice (CCA) Chief Counsel Advice (CCAs) are legal memoranda from the IRS Office of Chief Counsel that offer internal guidance on complex or uncertain legal issues. They help IRS employees apply the law consistently across audits and litigation. CCAs are not precedential and should not be cited as precedent. Because they are not published in the Internal Revenue Bulletin, they cannot be relied on, used, or cited as precedent in the disposition of other cases, but they may still help practitioners understand IRS reasoning and are often consulted for audit readiness or policy forecasting. Together, these documents form the administrative bridge between statute and taxpayer application, influencing everything from safe harbor compliance to procedural elections. Yet, even the most detailed guidance may leave open questions, and that's where the courts come in. When Does Judicial Authority Apply in Tax Research? The Role of Case Law in Federal Tax Interpretation Judicial authority refers to the body of federal court decisions that interpret tax statutes and administrative guidance. These opinions arise when disputes between taxpayers and the IRS are brought before the courts, usually because statutory or administrative guidance is unclear or contested. Through these decisions, courts clarify ambiguous provisions, resolve conflicts in interpretation, and create legal precedent, which tax professionals can rely on when evaluating the defensibility of a tax position. The role of the courts became even more central after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024): because courts must now exercise independent judgment rather than defer to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes, judicial decisions carry greater weight in fixing the meaning of the Code, and Treasury and IRS positions are more open to challenge than they were under *Chevron*. While judicial authority cannot override the IRC, absent an unconstitutional provision, it can influence how the Code is applied in practice and may determine whether a position meets the substantial authority standard. Case law is particularly valuable in gray areas where Treasury Regulations or IRS guidance are silent or inconsistent. It also plays a critical role in shaping the outcome of tax litigation and influencing how the IRS approaches enforcement. The U.S. Tax Court The U.S. Tax Court is generally the primary forum for federal tax disputes and offers a unique procedural advantage: taxpayers can bring a case without first paying the disputed tax liability. Key features of the Tax Court include: Exclusive focus on tax matters Judges with deep subject-matter expertise Nationwide jurisdiction Opinions that may be cited as precedent, including regular opinions and memorandum opinions; summary opinions are different and are not precedential Decisions appealable to the U.S. Courts of Appeals Because of the volume and focus of Tax Court rulings, they are among the most frequently referenced sources in federal tax research, particularly when interpreting ambiguous IRC sections or resolving inconsistencies in administrative guidance. Other Federal Courts In addition to the Tax Court, tax disputes may be resolved in other federal forums, depending on the circumstances: U.S. District Courts – Generally hear refund suits after payment of the disputed tax; allow jury trials U.S. Court of Federal Claims – Handles refund suits and monetary claims against the federal government U.S. Courts of Appeals – Hear appeals from trial-level courts; interpretations may vary across circuits U.S. Supreme Court – Final authority on all federal law; rarely hears tax cases, but its decisions are binding on all courts nationwide Each court adds to the evolving interpretation of federal tax law. Because rulings can differ across circuits, practitioners must evaluate precedential weight and jurisdictional relevance when citing judicial authority in support of a position.

title: 10 best AP automation software tools
summary: Compare the best AP automation software for procurement and finance teams, including AI features, ERP fit, invoice processing, and payments.
body_text: Accounts payable (AP) teams are still losing time to manual invoice work, even as AI has made invoice capture, general ledger (GL) coding, purchase order (PO) matching, and exception handling more automated. Ardent Partners data cited by Tungsten Automation shows the gap clearly: Best-in-class AP teams process invoices for $2.78 each , with a 49.2% straight-through processing rate. The average team pays $9.40 per invoice and reaches a 32.6% touchless rate. Choosing the right AP automation software in 2026 means looking past basic invoice routing. The best platforms can handle messy, real-world invoice volume and prevent exceptions earlier by connecting AP to the business context behind each invoice. Below, we compare 10 platforms and show where AI capability should shape your shortlist. Key takeaways AP automation software replaces manual invoice handling with a system that processes the majority of invoices without human touch. The 10 platforms in this guide are split into three categories: end-to-end procure-to-pay platforms, AP-specialist tools, and ERP-native modules. Best-in-class AP teams process invoices for $2.78 each at a 49.2% touchless rate, while the average cost per invoice is $9.40 at a touchless rate of 32.6%. In 2026, the buying decision is increasingly about how high a touchless rate the platform's AI can sustain on real-world, exception-heavy invoice volume. Zip connects invoice coding and PO matching with the intake, approval, and contract context behind every request. Enterprise customers have processed more than $500 billion in spend and saved over $9 billion. Read Zip's AP acceleration guide for more ways to modernize invoice processing. Best AP automation software at a glance The 10 platforms below cover three distinct buyer profiles: end-to-end procure-to-pay (Zip, Ivalua, JAGGAER); AP-specialist tools (Stampli, Tipalti, AvidXchange, Nanonets, Airbase by Paylocity); and enterprise resource planning (ERP) native modules (NetSuite, Sage Intacct). Please note that these are not listed in any specific order. Software Best for G2 rating AI capability Ideal company size Zip End-to-end orchestration from intake through payment, with an AI agent fleet 4.6 ★ AI invoice coding, AI risk detection, AI data validation, AI vendor consolidation, automated PO matching Mid-market and enterprise NetSuite AP automation inside an Oracle/NetSuite ERP footprint 4.1 ★ Built-in OCR, NetSuite Bill Capture Mid-market to enterprise NetSuite shops Ivalua Source-to-pay buyers with complex direct-materials needs 4.3 ★ Configurable AI in capture and matching Enterprise Nanonets Fast, lightweight AI invoice processing 4.7 ★ Intelligent document processing (IDP) SMB to mid-market Airbase by Paylocity Unified card + bill + expense in one tool 4.4 ★ AI bill auto-coding SMB to mid-market AvidXchange Middle-market companies replacing paper checks 4.4 ★ Capture + AvidPay supplier network Middle market JAGGAER Source-to-pay (S2P) with regulated-industry compliance 4.1 ★ Configurable AI across S2P Enterprise Sage Intacct AP for Sage Intacct accounting customers 4.3 ★ AI-powered data extraction inside Intacct Mid-market Stampli Conversation-first AP with all comms on the invoice 4.6 ★ Billy, an AI assistant (coding, dup detection, anomaly flags) SMB to mid-market Tipalti Global payables across many subsidiaries and currencies 4.5 ★ AI invoice capture + tax + supplier onboarding Mid-market to enterprise What does good AP automation look like in 2026? Good AP automation in 2026 raises touchless invoice processing as close as possible to the 49.2% best-in-class benchmark, while using AI to handle the exceptions that rules-based systems can't. The best platforms reduce manual work, lower invoice processing costs, and shorten cycle times without forcing AP teams to resolve the same issues repeatedly. According to the Ardent Partners data, top-performing AP teams can process 49.2% of invoices straight-through, or "touchless," compared to a 32.6% industry average. They also process each invoice for around $2.78, while the average team pays $9.40. Cycle time shows a similar gap: Best-in-class teams can clear an invoice in 3.1 days compared to 17.4 days on average. AP teams have to ask themselves how high their AP software's AI can raise their touchless rate before it plateaus. In practice, that ceiling is set by three things: how clean the invoice data is when it arrives, how well the platform's AI codes and matches non-standard invoices, and how it resolves exceptions when matching fails. The 10 platforms provide solutions in very different ways. 10 best AP automation software platforms We've evaluated each platform by fit, core strengths, and the AI capabilities that impact AP performance the most. 1. Zip Best for: End-to-end orchestration from intake through payment, with AI built for procurement and AP work. Zip is the only platform on this list that automates AP from the moment a purchase is requested. That can be a significant advantage since invoice exceptions usually start upstream. If the intake request, PO, contract, or supplier record is incomplete, optical character recognition (OCR) can only do so much once the invoice reaches AP. Zip captures that context earlier, then applies AI invoice coding, PO matching, and exception detection when the invoice is ready for review. The biggest advantage of Zip for finance teams is its AI agent fleet . The platform offers 50+ purpose-built AI agents, including AI Invoice Coding, Data Validation, AI Risk Detection, Preferred Vendor, and AI Vendor Consolidation. These agents work inside approval flows, so teams can review AI actions alongside the same controls, audit trails, and routing logic they already use. Zip also connects with major ERPs, including NetSuite, Sage Intacct, Workday, and Oracle, and supports payments in 60+ currencies across 200+ countries. Zip is not the lightest tool in this guide. A small team that needs a five-seat invoice tool for QuickBooks may be better served by Stampli or Nanonets. But for finance and procurement leaders who need AP to scale with the rest of the business, Zip is the stronger fit. It's built for higher-volume, cross-functional workflows where upstream context determines how smoothly invoices move. Key features: Intake-to-pay orchestration: Zip captures spend details at the request stage, tying AP to the broader procurement orchestration process that shapes the PO, contract, supplier record, and approved budget. AI invoice coding: Zip adapts to your chart of accounts and historical coding patterns and learns from corrections over time. AI fleet for AP: Data Validation, AI Risk Detection, Preferred Vendor, AI Vendor Consolidation, and other agents operate inside your current approval process. Automated PO matching: Zip supports three-way matching with configurable tolerances and routing for exceptions. Customizable approvals: Teams can route approvals by amount, department, vendor, contract type, or risk score. Global payments: Zip supports 60+ currencies, 200+ countries, and 110+ local clearing systems. Audit trail: Every AI action, approval, and exception is logged for review. G2 rating: 4.6 stars See how AP teams can move faster, reduce manual invoice work, and improve payment workflows in Zip's guide: AP Accelerated: A two-part AI framework for finance leaders 2. NetSuite Best for: AP automation inside an Oracle/NetSuite ERP footprint, where consolidating AP into the core financials platform is more important than best-in-class AP-specialist features. NetSuite's popular cloud ERP platform includes an AP automation solution that's built right in. Because it's part of a larger system that also handles things like financials, purchasing, and vendor info, it aims to give businesses more visibility, control, and efficiency throughout their entire procure-to-pay process , all within one system. Because it's a full ERP, some buyers find more features and cost than they need for an AP-only project. The tradeoff is that as your needs evolve, the integrated capabilities are already there, without a second implementation. Key features: Unified ERP platform: NetSuite's AP automation tool is a component of its broader cloud-based ERP system. This means AP processes are integrated with other key business functions like GL, customer relationship management (CRM) tools, and supply chain management. Native integration with procurement: The platform includes built-in procurement capabilities, like purchase order creation and matching, to help streamline the process from initial order to final payment within the same system. Customizable workflows: NetSuite allows for the configuration of approval processes for invoices and payments. These workflows can often be tailored to match specific organizational structures and internal control requirements. Comprehensive vendor management: The system provides tools for managing vendor information, including tracking details, purchase history, and payment terms. Scalable: As a cloud-based platform, NetSuite is designed to accommodate business growth and increasing transaction volumes. The system's infrastructure can typically adapt to handle larger amounts of data and users as needed. G2 rating: 4.1 stars 3. Ivalua Best for: Source-to-pay buyers in complex direct-materials industries (manufacturing, automotive, life sciences) that need deep configuration more than fast deployment. Ivalua offers an adaptable platform for automating your accounts payable processes, and what often sets it apart is its ability to be configured to your specific needs. Beyond AP automation, Ivalua stands out for its e-purchasing and contract management capabilities. It offers businesses a more unified approach to the entire buying and paying cycle. It's worth noting that this depth can be more than an AP-only buyer needs. Teams looking for a quick invoice capture and approval tool might find Ivalua's implementation lift and configuration requirements too heavy. Some reviews have also mentioned that the customer service and technical support could be improved. Key features: Highly adaptable platform: Ivalua's no-code/low-code platform allows for heavy customization to match unique and evolving business processes with no coding experience required. Comprehensive CLM integrated with source-to-pay: Ivalua offers a complete CLM module built into its broader source-to-pay suite. Contract terms can carry into procurement activity, giving teams more control from sourcing through supplier management. Supplier collaboration tools: Ivalua provides a dedicated supplier portal with various features designed to foster deep collaboration with suppliers. This includes shared workspaces, performance management tools, and direct communication channels. Focus on direct materials management: While also strong in indirect procurement , Ivalua is often noted for its capabilities in managing direct materials. G2 rating: 4.3 stars 4. Nanonets Best for: Small to medium-sized businesses (SMBs) and mid-market teams that primarily need AI-powered invoice capture and coding rather than full procurement. Nanonets offers a focused approach to AP automation through AI-powered document processing. Teams can feed invoices into the platform from scanned files, email, or digital formats, and its AI extracts key fields such as vendor names, invoice numbers, amounts, and line items. From there, Nanonets supports custom approval and routing rules, so invoices move through review based on your company's process. Nanonets' focused approach to AI-powered invoice processing best suits small-to-mid-market teams that need OCR-grade capture without a full P2P rollout. Companies with multi-entity, multi-currency, or contract-driven procurement needs, however, will hit Nanonets' ceiling quickly. Key features: Intelligent document processing (IDP) focus: Nanonets' core technology centers around understanding the context and structure of documents, aiming to go beyond basic OCR. AI-powered data extraction: Nanonets emphasizes its AI's ability to achieve high accuracy in extracting data from invoices and other financial documents with a relatively small initial training dataset. No-code/low-code customization: The platform offers a user interface that allows for creating and modifying data extraction rules and workflows with minimal to no coding required. Developer-friendly application programming interface (API): For more advanced users and integrations, Nanonets offers a comprehensive API for custom development and deeper connectivity with other systems. G2 rating: 4.7 stars 5. Airbase by Paylocity Best for: SMBs and mid-market teams already using Paylocity's human capital management (HCM) platform that want corporate cards, AP, and expense management in one tool. Airbase, acquired by Paylocity in October 2024, brings AP automation together with corporate cards and employee expense reports. For AP, teams can upload or email invoices, set approval rules that match their card and expense policies, and pay suppliers electronically. Paylocity frames the combined product around managing payroll and non-payroll spend from one platform. If you don't already use Paylocity, or don't plan to manage cards, expenses, and AP on one platform, some of Airbase's advantages are less relevant. Buyers who need source-to-pay or complex multi-entity AP may also find the platform on the lighter end of the market. Key features: Unified spend management: Airbase combines virtual and physical corporate cards with AP automation and expense management in a single interface so you don't need to juggle multiple systems. Integrated approval workflows: The platform lets you create unified approval workflows that can be applied consistently across all spending types, from card requests to expense reports. Real-time visibility across all spend: By having all spending data in one place, Airbase offers a comprehensive, real-time view of where your money is going. Automated accounting: Airbase automates the syncing of transaction data from cards, bills, and expenses directly to the general ledger. G2 rating (Paylocity): 4.4 stars 6. AvidXchange Best for: Middle-market companies that still pay a high share of suppliers by paper check and want a partner with a turnkey supplier-enablement team. If you're tired of printing and mailing paper checks and want to transition more of your suppliers to electronic payments, AvidXchange's AvidPay Network, along with its dedicated supplier services team, could be a major advantage. The platform's focus on building out this two-sided network aims to make the payment experience smoother for both your AP team and your suppliers. While AvidXchange does offer other AP automation features like invoice processing, the real value lies in its extensive supplier network for efficient electronic payments. But if a good chunk of your suppliers are unwilling or unable to join the network, it'll be difficult to reap the rewards. Businesses with a substantial number of suppliers, specifically those open to electronic payments, would benefit the most from this software. Key features: AvidPay Network: This is the core of AvidXchange's network, facilitating electronic payments to a large community of suppliers. This can lead to faster payments for suppliers and reduced paper check processing for buyers. Supplier services team: AvidXchange has a dedicated team focused on onboarding and supporting suppliers within its network, encouraging adoption of electronic payment methods. This reduces the burden on the buyer's AP team to manage supplier transitions. Multiple payment options: The platform supports various electronic payment methods within its network, giving suppliers flexibility in how they receive funds. Focus on the middle market: This AP automation tool is tailored specifically for the needs of middle-market businesses and their often diverse supplier base. G2 rating: 4.4 stars 7. JAGGAER Best for: Enterprise S2P buyers in regulated industries (manufacturing, life sciences, public sector) with direct-materials and complex compliance requirements. JAGGAER offers AP automation as a fully integrated component within its broader source-to-pay platform. This means that your invoice processing and payment workflows can cleanly connect with your sourcing, contract management, and e-procurement activities. It's all within the same system. Because JAGGAER is designed for end-to-end procurement, businesses that want a standalone AP automation solution might find its extensive capabilities more than they need. Implementing the system may also involve a lot more time and effort compared to simpler AP-specific tools. However, JAGGAER is often recognized for its ability to handle complex procurement scenarios and is used across various industries, including those with intricate direct materials requirements and unique compliance needs . Key features: Unified source-to-pay platform: JAGGAER offers a comprehensive suite where AP automation is a native part of a broader system encompassing sourcing, contract management, and e-procurement. Strategic sourcing capabilities: Beyond just processing invoices, JAGGAER provides tools for strategic sourcing , including advanced analytics, supplier management, and e-sourcing functionalities. Direct materials management: JAGGAER is designed to handle the complexities of direct materials procurement, catering to industries with intricate supply chains and production needs. This includes features for managing complex bills of materials and integrating procurement with production planning. Supplier collaboration focus: The platform includes tools and functionalities designed to improve communication, collaboration, and supplier relationship management (SRM) throughout the entire lifecycle. G2 rating: 4.1 stars 8. Sage Intacct Best for: Mid-market finance teams already standardized on Sage Intacct who want native AP rather than a bolt-on. Sage Intacct's AP automation software often centers on deep and native integration within its broader cloud financial management platform. Unlike some solutions that bolt onto an accounting system, Sage Intacct's AP automation is designed to work in conjunction with its core financials as a unified, real-time view of your financial data. The consolidated platform eliminates the need for separate integrations, which results in a smoother process and a more consistent financial overview. However, companies needing highly specialized AP features beyond core accounting-centric automation might find it less flexible than dedicated AP solutions. Key features: Native integration with cloud financials: Sage Intacct's AP automation is built directly into its core accounting platform, so there's an uninterrupted flow of financial data. AI-powered intelligent data extraction within accounting workflows: The software uses AI to automate invoice data capture directly within the AP bill entry process. Multi-entity AP management: For organizations with multiple legal entities, Sage Intacct offers sophisticated features to manage AP processes across entities from a centralized system, including intercompany accounting and consolidated reporting. Configurable approval workflows aligned with financial controls: This platform lets teams create detailed and customizable approval workflows for invoices that can be directly tied to their overall financial controls and organizational structure within the accounting system. G2 rating: 4.3 stars 9. Stampli Best for: SMB to mid-market AP teams that prioritize ease of use, fast adoption, and keeping all of their invoice conversations in one thread. Stampli stands out for bringing AP communication and documentation directly onto the invoice itself. Controllers can see the history of an invoice, who approved it, and which questions or comments came up during review. Stampli's AI assistant, Billy, automates routine AP tasks, including coding suggestions, duplicate detection, anomaly flags, and approval routing, and is one of the more recognizable named AI capabilities in this category. While generally praised for its user-friendliness and collaboration features, some third-party reviews have occasionally mentioned that Stampli's reporting capabilities, while functional, might not be quite as customizable or advanced as those found in more enterprise-focused or accounting-centric AP solutions. However, Stampli is often a great fit for small to mid-sized companies that value ease of use and clear communication across departments involved in AP. Key features: Centralized communication hub on the invoice: Stampli's interface is designed to keep all communication, approvals, and documentation directly linked to each specific invoice image, so you won't need to switch between emails or separate communication tools to understand the context of an invoice. AI assistant: Billy, Stampli's proprietary AI, learns your specific AP processes to automate tasks like invoice coding, approval routing, and identifying potential duplicate invoices. User-friendly interface: Stampli is frequently praised for its ease of use and simple design, requiring minimal training for both AP teams and approvers across the organization. Direct vendor communication: Stampli allows for direct communication with vendors regarding specific invoices from within the platform, centralizing vendor queries and responses. G2 rating: 4.6 stars 10. Tipalti Best for: Mid-market and enterprise teams with global supplier bases, multi-entity operations, and heavy cross-border tax compliance. For businesses going through rapid international growth or those with complex, multi-subsidiary operations, Tipalti's AP automation software is a good fit. It's designed to handle global supplier relationships and spend. Procurement teams can make sure suppliers are onboarded efficiently through the self-service portal, paid accurately in their local currencies via various methods, and remain compliant with tax regulations, all within one system. It's worth noting that some users find the platform relatively expensive, especially for smaller businesses, and the initial setup might take some time. Despite these potential drawbacks, the efficiency gains from Tipalti's global payment capabilities and the simple supplier onboarding can greatly reduce administrative overhead and strengthen international supplier relationships. Key features: Global payment engine: Tipalti supports global payments across 200+ countries with 50+ payment methods, including ACH, wire, PayPal, and local rails. Multi-entity management: The platform is specifically designed to handle the complexities of organizations with multiple subsidiaries or entities, allowing for centralized management of AP processes, payment workflows, and reporting across the entire corporate structure. Integrated tax and regulatory compliance: Tipalti incorporates built-in features to manage global tax compliance, including W-9/W-8 collection, TIN matching, and OFAC screening. Self-service supplier portal: Tipalti provides a comprehensive portal where suppliers can self-manage their onboarding, payment preferences, and tax information. G2 rating: 4.5 stars How to choose an AP automation solution for your business Finding the right AP automation requires a bit of legwork. Let's explore some practical things to keep in mind as you figure out what truly fits your business. Know your needs and pain points Before you even consider any software demos, take a good look at what's slowing you down right now. What's complicating the current AP process? Is it the endless cycle of typing in invoice details, the frustration of chasing down approvals, or the mystery of where a payment actually is? Pinpointing these inefficiencies is the very first step. Understanding your current AP journey will shed light on the specific features you need in an automation solution. What works (and what doesn't) for a small, local business will look very different from the priorities of a larger company dealing with multiple entities and complex approval hierarchies. Evaluate your current system Once you've got a handle on your pain points, the next step is to think about how a new AP automation solution will play with the tools you already use. Your AP process likely doesn't live in isolation. Do you have a separate system for managing purchase orders or contracts? What about where your invoices are stored before they enter the AP workflow? Consider how easily a new solution can connect with these existing platforms. Think beyond just the immediate integrations, too. As your business evolves, you might adopt new software. Understand if a potential AP automation solution offers open APIs . This flexibility can save you a lot of headaches down the road, allowing for smoother data flow and a more connected overall business ecosystem. Consider vendor reputation and support Choosing an AP automation partner means you also have to look at the company behind it. Before you commit, do a little digging into its reputation. Online reviews and customer stories can offer valuable insights into the brand's reliability and how well it supports its customers. Don't underestimate the importance of responsive and helpful customer support. When questions arise or you encounter a technical snag, you'll want to know that help is readily available. Consider the support channels on offer (phone, email, chat), the response times, and if the company provides adequate training and onboarding resources. A strong supplier with excellent support can make all the difference in ensuring a smooth implementation and a positive long-term experience. Understand pricing and ROI Getting a handle on the cost of an AP automation solution means looking beyond the sticker price. You'll want to review the different pricing models, too. Is it per invoice, per user, or a tiered structure? Make sure you understand what you're paying for and how it aligns with your transaction volume and team size. Beyond the initial outlay, really consider the potential return on investment (ROI) . Think about the time your team currently spends on manual tasks and how much you could save by automating data entry and approvals. Factor in the cost of errors, late payment penalties, and the potential to snag early payment discounts. Don't forget to ask about any hidden costs, like implementation fees or charges for integrating with your other systems. As a sanity check on ROI math, consider Ardent Partners' 2025 benchmarks that peg the spread between average and best-in-class AP processing at $6.62 per invoice ($9.40 average vs. $2.78 best-in-class). Multiply by your annual invoice volume to size the prize. Request demos and pilot programs Once you've narrowed down your options, don't hesitate to request personalized demos. This is your chance to see the software in action, tailored to your specific workflows and pain points. Pay close attention to the user interface: Is it intuitive and easy to navigate? Can you envision your team quickly adopting it? Even better than a demo is a pilot program, if the provider offers one. This lets you test the software in your actual environment with real data, albeit often on a limited scale. A pilot provides invaluable insights into how the solution integrates with your existing systems, how your team adapts to it, and the tangible benefits it delivers. It's a fantastic way to de-risk your decision and ensure the solution truly meets your needs. Future-proof your decision Beyond solving today's AP challenges, picking the right automation solution sets your business up for future success. Think about where your company is headed, and make sure the solution you choose can easily scale to accommodate these changes without becoming a bottleneck itself. Think beyond scalability and evaluate the vendor's long-term vision, too. Is the company actively investing in research and development? Does it have a clear roadmap for new features and improvements? A supplier committed to innovation is more likely to provide a solution that remains cutting-edge and continues to meet your evolving needs. Asking about future plans can give you confidence that your investment will continue to deliver value as your business grows and technology advances. In 2026, the most important roadmap question is whether the vendor's AI is built to lift your touchless processing rate over time, or whether it plateaus at the rules-based ceiling. How Zip wins on AP automation The 10 platforms above each have a profile they're built for, and Zip's profile is ideal for finance teams that want AP automation tied into the rest of procurement, with a fleet of AI agents doing the work. Three things separate Zip in this category: AP starts at intake. Zip captures clean data the moment a purchase is requested. By the time an invoice arrives, the PO, contract, and supplier record are already aligned. That upstream cleanliness is what lets Zip's AI hit higher touchless rates than tools that only see the invoice. Named AI agents rather than a single chatbot. Zip's 50+ AI agents include AI Invoice Coding, Data Validation, AI Risk Detection, Preferred Vendor, and AI Vendor Consolidation. Each runs inside the workflow with a full audit trail. Built for enterprise scale. Zip processes payments in 60+ currencies across 200+ countries with 110+ local clearing systems, and integrates with NetSuite, Sage Intacct, Oracle, and Workday. Enterprise customers using Zip have collectively saved more than $9 billion and processed over $500 billion in spend. If your evaluation criteria are "AI ceiling, end-to-end visibility, and enterprise-grade controls," Zip is built for your shortlist. Request a personalized demo to see Zip's AP automation and AI agents on your own invoices. Frequently asked questions What is AP automation software? AP automation software reduces the manual work involved in invoice capture, data extraction, coding, matching, approvals, and payment. Modern platforms use AI to read invoices, match them to purchase orders, route exceptions, and post approved invoices to the ERP. The goal is to shorten invoice cycle time and raise the share of invoices that move through AP without human intervention. What is touchless invoice processing? Touchless invoice processing is the percentage of invoices that move from receipt to ERP posting without human involvement. According to Ardent Partners data cited by Tungsten Automation, the industry average is 32.6%, while best-in-class AP teams sit at 49.2%. Stronger AI can raise that ceiling by handling invoice exceptions that rules-based matching often sends back to AP. How much does AP automation save? Top-performing AP teams process invoices for $2.78 each, compared with the $9.40 industry average, which saves $6.62 per invoice. For a company processing 10,000 invoices a year, that would mean roughly $66,200 in annual processing savings. The Ardent Partners study also noted that best-in-class teams clear invoices in 3.1 days, compared with 17.4 days on average. For a rough estimate, multiply your per-invoice cost gap by your annual invoice volume. What's the difference between AP automation and procure-to-pay software? AP automation covers the invoice-to-payment process. It captures invoices, codes line items, matches invoices to purchase orders, routes approvals, and supports payment. Procure-to-pay software covers the broader process, starting with intake, sourcing, supplier onboarding, contracts, and purchase orders. Platforms like Zip include AP automation, but also manage the upstream context that determines whether an invoice arrives clean. Does AP automation software work with my ERP? Yes, most major AP automation platforms integrate with leading ERPs and accounting systems. Common connectors include NetSuite, Sage Intacct, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Workday, Oracle, QuickBooks, and Xero. Before choosing a vendor, confirm which fields sync, how often data updates, and whether the integration supports two-way communication. ERP-native AP modules are another option for teams that prefer one core system. What should I look for in AP automation software in 2026? Look for AP automation software that can improve touchless processing on real invoice volume. The most important factors are AI accuracy, ERP fit, approval control, global payment coverage, and whether the platform connects AP to upstream procurement data. The last feature is important because invoice exceptions often start with missing approvals, incomplete supplier records, or mismatched purchase orders. title: ML Jobs in Snowflake Data Clean Rooms Now GA
summary: ML Jobs in Snowflake Data Clean Rooms is now generally available, enabling collaborative model training and scoring across multiparty data without moving raw records.
body_text: Until now, running complex ML workloads inside a data clean room meant hitting a wall. Most clean room environments are limited to SQL queries or single-node Python, which runs into memory constraints quickly at enterprise data volumes. Teams ended up treating clean rooms as a compliance tool rather than a place to build models. ML Jobs changes that. ML Jobs in Snowflake Data Clean Rooms™ is now generally available. Data scientists can now bring their standard Python ML stack with distributed training, hyperparameter optimization, custom packages and GPU compute directly into a multiparty collaboration. Models train on combined data from multiple organizations without raw records leaving anyone's account, and the pipeline runs automatically rather than requiring manual intervention each time. Consider a concrete example from advertising. An advertiser builds audience and measurement models using ad log data from publishers, identity resolution data from identity providers and transaction signals from retail data partners. Each data source improves model quality. However, each provider has legitimate concerns about how their data is used and who can see it. At the same time, the advertiser's model logic and scoring algorithms are proprietary IP they have no interest in exposing to their data partners. ML Jobs in Data Clean Rooms gives each party what they need. Data and identity providers know their data is governed and used only for workloads they have explicitly approved. The advertiser's model code stays inside the collaboration boundary, invisible to the data providers. As new data flows in, models score continuously on fresh signals without any party renegotiating access or re-exposing their assets. The same infrastructure also points toward what's next: training AI agents whose effectiveness depends on signals distributed across multiple organizations. This includes a publisher's behavioral data, an advertiser's conversion history, a data provider's demographic enrichment, all combined in a single fine-tuning run inside a governed clean room. That's where multiparty ML is heading, and the foundation is available today. “Snowflake's ML Jobs release in DCR enabled us to bring VideoAmp's best-in-class lift methodology into a dramatically more scalable computing environment. We can now process lift reports faster, using more signals than ever before — unlocking greater value for our clients at scale.” —Katy Mitchell, Sr Director Ad Measurement Products, VideoAmp "At Affinity Solutions, we're proud to use ML Jobs in Snowflake Data Clean Rooms. For advertisers, the ability to train and score models on combined data without raw records leaving anyone's environment solves a problem that has blocked serious measurement and targeting work for years. What excites us most is the foundation this creates for what's next: AI agents continuously trained on our consumer purchase data and our clients' data in a safe, secure and seamless way. ML Jobs makes data collaboration genuinely practical, and that's what the future of advertising will be built on.” —Kalyan Lanka, Chief Product Officer, Affinity Solutions "With Snowflake's ML Jobs now available in Snowflake's Data Clean Room Collaboration API, Kroger Precision Marketing is able to connect our industry-leading media measurement sciences natively within Snowflake Data Clean Rooms. This innovation unlocks our best-in-class incrementality sciences, allowing KPM to deliver trusted, privacy-first insights at the speed and scale modern marketers demand." —Nathan Dall, Product, Data Collaboration & AI, Kroger Precision Marketing What this enables Some of the most valuable ML models in advertising, financial services and healthcare require data from multiple organizations that have generally not been able to share it because moving it across company boundaries creates privacy, or competitive problems. Clean room ML is designed to address that directly. Multiparty model training and scoring A machine learning model trained on a single data silo reflects only that silo's view of the world. A retail media network, a financial services provider and a brand each have distinct signals about consumer behavior such as purchase history, transaction patterns and engagement data that are far more predictive in combination than in isolation. ML Jobs makes it practical to run a single training pipeline across feature sets from multiple parties. Each organization contributes to the model without exposing raw records to the others. The accuracy improvement from richer, multi-source features is one of the clearest arguments for collaborative ML. Propensity scoring is a direct example of this. A publisher scores their full user population for purchase propensity on behalf of an advertiser, but a propensity model trained only on the publisher's behavioral signals is limited. Bring in the advertiser's first-party conversion history and a data provider's demographic and psychographic signals, and the same model trains on a far richer feature set: content affinity and session behavior from the publisher, income tier and life stage from the data provider, and actual purchase outcomes from the advertiser. The resulting scores are meaningfully more predictive because the model has seen the full picture of what drives conversion. Models that previously relied on a single publisher's behavioral signals can now be retrained with each new campaign using the full set of available features, keeping scores fresh rather than degrading as audience composition shifts. Ease of development, deployment and scale For ML engineers and data scientists, the experience inside a clean room collaboration is the same as outside it: Write standard Python, use any packages you need and work in whatever IDE or notebook environment you prefer. The only addition is a short YAML code spec that declares what to run and what it needs: ml_jobs: - name: train_model entrypoint: train.py stage_code_dir: '@my_db.public.ml_stage/project' pip_requirements: - xgboost - scikit-learn - pandas No Docker images to build, no container registries to configure, no infrastructure to provision manually. Scaling to multiple nodes or GPUs is a parameter change, not an architectural rewrite. Registering a new version of a job, updating requirements or adding a pipeline step is a spec change. Once a template is approved, it runs via a single SQL call from any orchestrator on whatever schedule you set. The development workflow is also designed to avoid friction at the clean room boundary. You can build and test the full ML Job workflow outside Snowflake Data Clean Rooms (DCR) in a standard Snowflake environment using the same Python scripts and container runtime. Once you’ve built and tested, you can bring it into the collaboration using the code spec with a pinned image version to lock down the versions of dependencies you have developed and tested with. This means iteration happens in your normal development environment, and you can seamlessly deploy and operationalize the workloads in DCR. ML Jobs workloads are designed to run as production pipelines, not one-off experiments. Once a template is approved, you can schedule it at any cadence, trigger it from upstream data events or orchestrate it from any automation tool such as Snowflake Tasks, Airflow or any system that can make a SQL call. Operationally, activity history for all job runs is also queryable in Snowflake, giving you an audit trail of analysis runs. And when something goes wrong, you can access the standard container logs for debugging by allowing monitoring on the ML Jobs. Use cases Incrementality measurement without a data intermediary Measuring true sales lift from advertising requires joining ad exposure data with purchase outcomes across party lines. Historically, this required a neutral third party to hold the combined data or significant custom infrastructure — high-friction paths that most advertisers skip. With ML Jobs, a brand and a retailer run an uplift model inside the collaboration: impression logs stay in the brand's account, transaction data stays in the retailer's account and the model trains on the join. Causal lift measurement, which previously required a dedicated data science project, becomes a repeatable per-campaign workflow. Campaign teams get a real signal on what's working, not a proxy metric. Retail media attribution at transaction scale Retailer transaction data is one of the most valuable signals for attribution, but has been practically inaccessible to media agencies and DSPs due to competitive sensitivities. ML Jobs lets the attribution model run where the data lives. The retailer's records never move. The model output including attribution weights and conversion lift estimates get shared downstream. Identity crosswalk for higher match rates Third-party cookie deprecation has reduced deterministic match rates significantly for many advertising programs. When hashed email or device ID coverage is partial, deterministic joins leave a large portion of the audience unmatched. Closing that gap requires joining first-party advertiser data such as customer relationship management (CRM) records and conversion history with third-party identity provider graphs that map device IDs, hashed emails and mobile ad IDs across publishers. Probabilistic identity resolution, a model trained to match records across ID spaces using behavioral and contextual signals, can recover meaningful match rate lift, but it requires scale and dedicated compute. ML Jobs provides that inside the clean room: An advertiser's first-party CRM data and a third-party identity provider's graph train a resolution model without either party's records leaving their account. Where deterministic joins leave large portions of the audience unmatched, a well-trained resolution model closes that gap and because the model can be retrained as ID coverage shifts, match rates don't simply degrade over time and stay degraded. From lookalike scoring to campaign optimization agents Lookalike modeling produces a ranked list of users who resemble a seed audience, a static score at a point in time. A campaign optimization agent goes further: Given a campaign brief, budget and objective, it reasons over combined signals from multiple parties to recommend which audience segments to target, in what context and at what bid level. The difference in training data is what makes this possible in a clean room. A lookalike model trains on a publisher's user features against an advertiser's seed audience. A campaign optimization agent trains on publisher behavioral signals, advertiser conversion history across multiple campaigns and product categories, and data provider demographic enrichment simultaneously. It learns not just which users look like past converters, but which combinations of audience context, demographic profile and campaign type drive conversion and generalizes that learning to new campaigns the model has never seen before. The three-party clean room provides the governance structure that makes all three parties willing to contribute: The publisher's behavioral data never leaves their account, the advertiser's conversion history and model logic stay within the collaboration boundary and the data provider's demographic graph is used only for the approved training workload. Two parties and a warehouse can build a lookalike model. A campaign optimization agent requires multiparty training data, GPU compute and the trust model that clean room ML provides. How it compares to other approaches Certain clean room platforms design their ML APIs around tailored use cases, such as lookalike audience generation or specific custom model formats. Others utilize centralized, shared notebook environments, which are well-suited for exploratory data science and manual collaborative review. ML Jobs in Snowflake Data Clean Rooms expands on these approaches by supporting standard, end-to-end Python ML workloads optimized for automated production pipelines. Data remains within each party's respective account, utilizing a hash-based approval system that enables seamless, automated re-runs without requiring manual intervention for every execution. Additionally, when both parties enable Cross-Cloud Auto-Fulfillment, workloads run seamlessly across different clouds and regions. To efficiently scale to the needs of each project, the analysis runner can select a compute pool directly within their account that matches the workload—ranging from standard or high-memory CPUs for large feature sets, to GPU instances for accelerated tasks like deep learning and LLM fine-tuning (in supported regions). Get started ML Jobs in Data Clean Rooms is now available for all Snowflake accounts with the Data Clean Rooms environment installed. No account-level enablement required. For ML engineers and data scientists: Two end-to-end examples are available, each with a sample data generator, SQL worksheets for both parties and Python training and scoring scripts you can run today: Lookalike audience modeling with ML Jobs : Advertiser trains a lookalike classifier on publisher user features and activates the scored audience. Multiparty incrementality measurement with automated hyperparameter optimization (HPO): Brand and retail media network run per-campaign uplift modeling with Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. For campaign managers and media buyers evaluating this for measurement or targeting workflows: The incrementality and lookalike examples above are the fastest way to understand what's possible. Share them with your data science or measurement team. The examples include everything needed to run end to end, and the workflow maps directly to standard campaign and activation patterns you're already using. Full reference documentation: ML Jobs in Data Clean Rooms .

title: Why Roof Estimating Remains a Major Bottleneck in Property Claims
summary: Roof estimating is detailed, repetitive work. Learn how XactGen Roofing helps claims teams create stronger estimates inside Xactimate.
body_text: Roofing claims are routine, but that doesn’t make them simple For many claims professionals, the roof estimate is where time disappears. Even when the damage is familiar, the estimate still demands a series of detailed steps, and those steps add up across thousands of claims. Roof costs are rising, even in quiet storm years Roofing is among the largest and most expensive categories in property claims, and the latest data shows the pressure is climbing. According to the 2026 Verisk U.S. Roof Report , average residential roof replacement costs reached $17,631 in 2025, with repair costs averaging $4,699. That represents increases of roughly 33% and 25% , respectively, over the prior four-year average. Severity rose even though overall claims volume fell nearly 20%. Volume matters, too. Roofing accounts for around 30% of all line items in claims estimates. When one category drives that much activity, even small inefficiencies in estimating create meaningful operational impact. Two findings show why this isn’t a one-season problem: Aging roof stock is widespread. As of 2025, 38% of U.S. residential homes show moderate to poor roof condition, often with visible defects that affect performance in severe weather. Hail risk is broadening. Sixteen states saw severe hail affect more than 20% percent of roofs in 2025, up from 12 states in 2024. Roof estimating is detailed work, not just data entry The challenge is not only that roof estimates take time. While the work is repetitive, the details are important, and consistency across claims is critical. Estimators and adjusters often need to translate measurement data into a complete, reviewable estimate while accounting for roof geometry, materials, waste, openings, estimate context, and carrier or company guidelines. Each step may be manageable on its own. Together, they can slow the broader claims workflow. Consistency adds another layer. Different users can interpret the same roof data differently, and estimate quality varies with experience, workload, and familiarity with roofing best practices. Under normal conditions, that variability leads to extra review cycles. During high-volume periods, it becomes a real constraint. Wind and hail make the bottleneck harder to ignore Wind and hail remain the dominant threats to roofs, and the cadence of frequent, smaller-scale events can age a roof faster than any single storm. As Tory Farney, vice president, Verisk Weather Solutions, put it, hail risk isn’t about one monster storm but the rhythm of repeated events that weaken a roof over time. That steady pressure means claims teams aren’t solving an occasional estimating challenge. They’re managing a recurring operational pain point that intensifies during catastrophe events, when adjusters and estimators must process more claims in less time. And because many of the wind and hail events driving roof severity fall below catastrophe thresholds, estimate efficiency matters during surge events and in everyday claims operations alike. What a better roofing workflow should deliver? A better roofing workflow should help teams use roof measurement data more efficiently, reduce repetitive manual entry, support more consistent line-item and quantity generation, and fit into the tools estimators and adjusters already know. The goal isn’t to remove expertise from the process. It’s to give users a stronger starting point so they spend less time building an estimate from scratch and more time reviewing, validating, and applying professional judgment. How XactGen Roofing™ supports the work Verisk’s XactGen Roofing is designed to help estimators complete work fast. Built inside Xactimate®, XactGen Roofing can reduce manual effort and support more consistent roof estimating workflows, while keeping the estimator or adjuster in control of review and finalization. Roof estimating will always require expertise, context, and professional review. But the manual effort behind building the starting estimate can improve. As replacement costs climb and hail risk broadens, claims teams have a clear opportunity to rethink an especially persistent bottleneck in property estimating.
